To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the intrinsic dimensionality of the neural representation of objects in the inferotemporal (IT) cortex is estimated to be 100, that there are two main types of IT neurons, one type that responds to the presence of a specific part of an object and one that responds to the whole object, and that these types of neurons form a continuum.

(i) the intrinsic dimensionality of population representation of objects within inferotemporal (IT) cortex is estimated to be about 100; (ii) the intrinsic dimension of object representation in IT cortex lies on a continuum between purely structural, partsbased representation and purely holistic representation; (iii) cognitive knowledge in the form semantic information and task-related information is fed back from perirhinaI and prefrontal cortices, providing high-level expectations to assist in the interpretation object stimuli;

the neural representation of objects in inferior temporal cortex is best described as a distributed, hierarchical representation with multiple levels of representation and a continuum between a parts-based and holistic description.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain represents and recognizes objects and with the role of cognitive knowledge in object recognition.
understanding how the neural representation of object information in inferotempital cortex is organized, and the functional significance of this organization for visual object recognition.
how information about objects is represented and integrated in the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the representation of objects in IT is complex and multifaceted.
inferotemporal neurons are not tuned to a particular object, but rather to a particular object representation, which may be a structural, holistic, or multimodal-based object representation.
object representations in inferotempital cortex are distributed across a continuum between parts- and holistic descriptions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have provided a framework for understanding the neural basis of object recognition, and that this understanding can be used to develop a theory of object recognition in the brain that is consistent with both neurophysiological and neuropsychological evidence.
the brain is a highly efficient and effective machine that uses a distributed, population-based representation for objects that is flexible and adaptive to the task at hand.

object recognition is not a simple process but rather is the result of the interaction of a number of factors, including the nature of the object stimulus, its intrinsic representation, the task at hand and the cognitive knowledge available to the individual.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain is not a black box.
the brain is not simply a pattern classifier but is capable of representing objects in a way that allows it to make use of a variety of different types of information to achieve object recognition.
object recognition is a highly complex and distributed process, involving multiple cortical and subcortical regions and multiple processes that operate at multiple spatial and temporal scales.
